default.narration:
Your room. The flat is empty because Mum is on nights.

It's the first hour you've had to yourself in a week, and it's fine, and you check your phone eleven times.

Tunde is training for something specific and doesn't make a thing of it.

Afterwards he asks you a direct question about what you're actually doing with yourself, and takes the answer seriously enough to be unsatisfied by it.

He isn't unkind. He just doesn't pretend.

Jay's annoyed for about four seconds — the specific annoyance of someone who wanted to be asked and hasn't decided how to be — and then tells you.

His sister has a course place. There's a deposit. The date has already been moved once and can't be again.

He tells it in pieces, out of order, and stops before the part where he explains what he's going to do about it. You notice him stop.

You walk. It's a good two hours and genuinely funny in places.

Twice, unprompted, Jay says he's fine.

The second one is what stays with you on the way home, because nobody says it twice.

bubbles.speaker: char.bola
bubbles.text: You're still putting something in Friday, yeah?

default.narration:
She says it lightly and once, which is worse than if she pushed, and then waits.

It is Tuesday.

She finds her keys where she left them, which takes a while.

Four minutes later the door goes and the flat is the flat again.

default.narration:
Half five, and you've been up since eleven, which you're aware of.

Mum is doing the thing she does before a shift — moving through the flat picking things up and putting them somewhere else, coat already half on. There is a letter on the side that has been there four days, face down, which is its own kind of statement.

She is not angry. She is doing sums in her head while talking about something else, and you can tell, because you've watched her do it since you were twelve.

Jay is on the walkway and has been for a while, which he does when he wants to be found without having asked.

He is funny for about ninety seconds and then isn't, and the gap between those two things is visible if you know him. Jay's flat is where you ate for a stretch when things were bad, and neither of you has ever said a word about it.

Tunde's message arrives while Jay is talking. *Cage, eight. You coming or not.*

Jay doesn't ask. That's the whole difficulty.

He describes the situation and then goes quiet and lets the silence do the asking, and both of you know exactly what is happening.

There is forty pounds in your pocket. The deposit is not forty pounds.

You put a container of somebody else's aunt's food in your own fridge, in a flat where the money is tight, on the day you decided what you were and weren't going to do about Jay's sister.

Mum's shoes are still not by the door.

bubbles.speaker: char.jay
bubbles.text: That one's your mum's. She likes the rice.

default.narration:
On the landing outside your flat, Jay splits it — one container for himself, one held out.



He says it like it's nothing, because to him it is. His aunt made too much, the way she has made too much for eleven years.

Jay is outside before you've finished getting ready, which is how you know it matters.

What he needs is a lift with an errand. His aunt has put food aside and it has to be picked up before she shuts at four, and it's a bus and a walk each way, and he doesn't want to do it on his own.

That's genuinely all he says.

They get back in the car and go. Four minutes, start to finish.

Nothing happened. Nothing is on any record anywhere. There is no charge, no note, no follow-up, and in a week nobody official will remember it at all.

Dee comes to you, which is not how it normally goes.

He is not a stranger. Two summers ago Dee got you a fortnight's work when you needed it, paid you on the Friday like he said he would, and drove you home the night the buses stopped. Neither of you has mentioned it since and neither of you needs to.

He's got a unit for a fortnight — phone cases, chargers, the usual — and he needs somebody on it Saturday, ten till six. Eighty quid, cash, end of the day.

He asks for you by name. He doesn't say why you, and it doesn't occur to him that he should, and eighty is a bit more than the day is worth.

Saturday is Saturday.

Two days since you decided what you were and weren't going to do about Jay's sister.

Jay hasn't messaged. That's not a falling-out; it's just Thursday. But it's the first morning since Sunday that you've woken up without somebody wanting something, and the quiet is not as good as you expected it to be.

default.narration:
Tunde finds you, which Tunde does, because Tunde plans things.

There's a trial. Saturday, ten till two, at the place he's been talking about since March. The man who runs it will be there and Tunde has already said your name — not put you forward formally, just said it, in the way that gets you looked at once.



He isn't selling it. He's about half embarrassed to have mentioned it, because he knows exactly how it sounds to say *there might be something in September* to somebody who needs money now.

Tunde talks about tomorrow like it's settled, because as far as he knows it is.

It's cold and neither of you goes back in for eleven minutes.

She says one thing about Tuesday. Not the money — Tuesday.

And then she talks about somebody's hip for the rest of the walk, and you can't tell whether the first thing was the point or whether you just made it the point.

Jay's mum has you by the arm inside six seconds and doesn't let go for another minute. You get introduced to two aunties as *the sensible one*, which is a thing she has called you since before it was true. There is a plate in your hand you don't remember accepting.

Mum is here. She knows this family. She is in the corner with Jay's mum and one of the aunties, and she has taken her shoes off, which you haven't seen her do since Christmas.

Through the doorway you can see the shape of the evening. Kai has the kitchen and four people. Jay is somewhere. Jay has been somewhere all evening.

bubbles.text: You're the only one round here I'd have him with.

Training's Tuesdays and Thursdays, six till half seven. Take him, bring him back, be about. Dee will sort you weekly for it.

At some point Jay says  — not as an accusation, just as a thing he knows — and after that it is easier rather than harder.

You have one afternoon and you can do one thing with it.

Not fix the week. Do one thing.

Nobody has messaged.

That is the first thing. Six days of somebody wanting something by four, and this morning the phone has one notification and it's the bank telling you what your balance is.

Mum went at six. The mug is washed.

The deposit was today and it either happened or it didn't, and you'll find out from somebody else rather than from Jay.

Tuesday is tomorrow, and a thirteen-year-old either has somebody coming or he hasn't.
